title: 〜ている

taeKim.title: Using the te-form for ongoing actions (〜ている)

summary: て-form + いる means either "is doing" or "is in the state of having done." Which one depends on the verb.
explanation: 〜ている is built from the て-form plus いる (to exist). Literally: "exists in the doing." It has two main jobs.
**1. Action in progress.** For verbs that take time — {食|た}べる, {練習|れんしゅう}する, {降|ふ}る, {待|ま}つ — 〜ている means "is doing right now." {今|いま}{曲|きょく}を{書|か}いています = I'm writing a piece right now.

**2. A state that resulted from a change.** For verbs that happen in an instant — {結婚|けっこん}する, {着|つ}く, {来|く}る, {開|あ}く, {知|し}る — 〜ている means the change happened and you're still in that state. {結婚|けっこん}しています = is married, not "is getting married." {来|き}ています = has come (and is here).
It also covers **habits**: {毎日|まいにち}ワニカニをやっています = I do WaniKani every day (these days).
Two things to remember: in casual speech the い drops ({食|た}べてる, {知|し}ってる), and the negative of {知|し}っている is {知|し}らない / {知|し}りません — never {知|し}っていない.

examples.ja: {今|いま}、{新|あたら}しい{曲|きょく}を{書|か}いています。
examples.en: I'm writing a new piece right now.

examples.note: 開く (to open) happened; the window stays open.

examples.ja: その{店|みせ}、{知|し}ってる？
examples.note: Casual: い dropped. 知る needs ている to mean "know."

examples.ja: {毎朝|まいあさ}コーヒーを{飲|の}んでいます。

a.ja: {来月|らいげつ}{結婚|けっこん}します。

contrasts.why: 結婚する is a one-time change. ます is the event itself; ている is the state you're in afterward.

b.ja: スザンナが{来|き}ています。

contrasts.why: 来る is arriving — instant. With ている she has arrived and is still here.

a.en: What will you do? / What do you do?

contrasts.why: Plain ます points to the future or to general habits. ている zooms in on what's happening now.

exercises.scene: Ranko asks about Susanna in late February.
exercises.prompt: スザンナはもう{東京|とうきょう}に＿＿。
exercises.en: Susanna is already in Tokyo. (She's come.)

options.why: 来る is an instant change (arriving). ている = she arrived and is still there. もう (already) fits perfectly.
This means she will come. Paired with もう (already), it clashes.
Past state — "she had come / was here." Implies she's no longer there, or that you're talking about an earlier time.

exercises.en: What are you doing right now?

options.why: 今 + ている asks about the action happening right now.
Grammatical, but it reads as "What will you do now?" — asking about plans, not what they're in the middle of.

exercises.scene: Someone uses a word you've never heard.
exercises.prompt: すみません、その{言葉|ことば}は＿＿。
exercises.en: Sorry, I don't know that word.

options.why: The negative of 知っている is 知らない / 知りません. It's an exception worth memorizing.
Looks logical, but it isn't used. Japanese says 知りません for "don't know."
This means "I know it" — the opposite of what you want.

exercises.en: The window is open. It's cold, isn't it.

options.why: 開く is an instant change. ている = it opened and is still open.
"The window will open" (or "opens") — describes the event, not the current state that's making it cold.

exercises.scene: Look outside and say it's raining right now.
exercises.why: Fresh observation → 雨が. 降っています for something happening now. 今 can sit at the front or right before the verb.

exercises.scene: Self-talk: say what you're doing right now, in one sentence.
exercises.model: {今|いま}、コーヒーを{飲|の}んでいます。
exercises.why: Any verb works: 今、〇〇をしています. Narrating like this, even in your head, is how thinking in Japanese starts.
